newsitem.title: GERMANY: NATO on agenda as Yeltsin flies in to meet Kohl.
newsitem.headline: NATO on agenda as Yeltsin flies in to meet Kohl.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin was due in this German spa once frequented by Russian nobility on Wednesday for talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl and to receive a "Man of the Year" award from German media.

The talks between the two leaders, their second meeting in three months, were likely to focus on intensive efforts to negotiate a charter defining Russia's relationship with the expanding NATO defence alliance.

Also certain to be discussed during the meeting on Thursday was the most awkward issue in relations between Russia and its closest friend in the West -- the fate of pricesless art treasures taken from Germany by the Red Army at the end of World War Two.

Presidential spokesman Sergey Yastrzhembsky said on Tuesday the meeting could have a significant effect on talks to agree a charter giving Russia a say in the Western alliance as it prepares to take in members from eastern Europe.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov failed to iron out their differences in talks in Moscow on Tuesday, and substantial issues remain to be resolved ahead of a July deadline both sides want to meet.
"It seems to me that the German chancellor is one of those Western politicians who are more sensitive to Russian arguments," Yastrzhembsky told Russian television.

"At this final stage of the drafting of an extremely important document, the chancellor's opinion is of particular importance, since I think the chancellor can speak very tellingly to his NATO partners after hearing the president's point of view," he said.
Whenever the two men meet, there is hope in Western capitals that Kohl, Russia's biggest advocate in the West, can use his warm personal ties with Yeltsin to ease strains with Moscow.

But even that friendship has failed to end a row over the vast collection of art shipped out of occupied Germany by Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin, including gold treasure excavated by German archeologist Heinrich Schliemann from ancient Troy.

The upper chamber of the Russian parliament was due to debate the issue on Wednesday, considering whether to back the lower house in overruling Yeltsin's veto of a draft law which says the art should stay in Russia.

There was some puzzlement in Germany over comments by Yeltsin, who told the weekly magazine Stern he would have some of the treasures in his luggage when he came. "Not the Troy gold of course," he said. "But I'll bring some other items with me."
Yeltsin, travelling with his wife Naina and his younger daughter Tatyana Dyachenko, was due to spend Wednesday evening in private before the formal part of the visit on Thursday.
Baden-Baden, a spa since Roman times, reached its heyday as a society resort in the 19th century.
Tsar Alexander II visited in 1863, as did many other nobles drawn by the waters and the famous casino, the setting of Fyodor Dostoyevsky's novel The Gambler.

Yeltsin and his family were staying in a luxury 19th century hotel with a river running through the grounds whose plush apartments cost $1,500 a night and which now occasionally welcomes some of Russia's nouveaux riches.
Yeltsin is due to receive a German media prize as "Man of the Year" for 1996 on Thursday evening and Kohl is scheduled to make a speech in praise of his friend.
Amid the pomp, two groups said they planned protests in Baden-Baden against alleged human rights abuse in Russia.
Amnesty International said it would urge Yeltsin to do more to protect critical journalists, of whom several had been killed or disappeared while reporting on the conflict in Chechnya.

And the Society for Threatened Peoples said the media award had tastelessly cast Yeltsin in a positive light only weeks after the end of the bloody conflict with Chechen rebels for which he shared responsibilty.
